intro.0: A measured step up from single-token drills. You will write several small objects that collaborate - one requests what it needs from another, each holds a single responsibility, and a class uses the collaborator it is given. No new theory is introduced here; these are the habits the SOLID drills build on.
task.1.title: Two objects collaborate
task.1.context: An object often produces a result by [[concept:pr-collaboration|delegating to a collaborator and acting on its response]]. Here a `Greeter` holds no notion of time itself - it queries a `Clock` for the hour and selects a greeting accordingly. The example below queries a `Sensor`; apply the same structure to the clock.
task.1.goal.0: Query the `clock` for the hour, then return `"Good morning"` when it is before 12 and `"Good afternoon"` otherwise.
task.1.goal.1: The clock reports 9, so the expected output is Good morning.
task.2.title: Request data from a collaborator
task.2.context:
A `Cart` should not hold prices - that responsibility belongs to the `PriceList`. The cart [[concept:pr-delegation|requests a price]] and multiplies it by the quantity. Retain the price list supplied to the cart, then query it.

The example below queries a `Catalog`; apply the same approach to the price list.
task.2.goal.0: Store the `prices` supplied to the constructor, then return the item's price multiplied by `qty`.
task.2.goal.1: A book costs 10 and qty is 3, so the expected output is 30.
task.3.title: A method with one responsibility
task.3.context: A well-formed method produces [[concept:pr-single-responsibility|a single, nameable result]]. `Area` performs exactly one calculation - the product of the two sides - and nothing more. The example below assigns one responsibility to a box; do the same for the rectangle.
task.3.goal.0: Return the area of the rectangle - `width` multiplied by `height`.
task.3.goal.1: For 4 by 5 the expected output is 20.
task.4.title: Assign each responsibility its own class
task.4.context:
`Checkout` was performing two responsibilities at once: the arithmetic (price multiplied by quantity) and the presentation (rendering that number as text). Two responsibilities in one method give it two reasons to change.

Move the presentation into `ReceiptFormatter`. `Checkout` retains the arithmetic and requests the text from the formatter. The example below separates a sale in the same way.
task.4.goal.0: Give `ReceiptFormatter` a `Format(int total)` that returns `"Total: "` followed by the total.
task.4.goal.1: In `Pay`, construct a formatter and request the text from it. For 10 by 2 the expected output is Total: 20.
task.5.title: Use an injected collaborator
task.5.context:
A class need not construct its own collaborators. `Mailer` receives an `Outbox` through its constructor and uses that instance - it never calls `new Outbox()` itself. A collaborator supplied from outside can be substituted later.

The example below supplies a `Printer` with its `Ink`; apply the same approach to the mailer and its outbox.
task.5.goal.0: Retain the `outbox` supplied to the constructor, then send `"hello "` followed by `who` through it.
task.5.goal.1: For Sam the expected output is sent: hello Sam.
task.6.title: Compose two objects and run
task.6.context:
Now assemble the pieces: a `Worker` receives a `ConsoleLog` and reports through it. Retain the log, then have `Report` write the status through the log it was given. Two small objects collaborating is the shape of most production code.

The example below composes a `Bell` with a `Speaker`; apply the same approach to the worker and its log.
task.6.goal.0: Retain the `log` supplied to the constructor, then write the `status` through it in `Report`.
task.6.goal.1: `Main` reports work done, so the expected output is work done.
task.7.title: Reading objects: summary
task.7.summaryIntro: You read and wrote several small objects that collaborate. These are the habits the SOLID drills build on.
task.7.summaryItems.0.title: Object collaboration -
task.7.summaryItems.0.text: one object requests what it needs from another, then acts on the response.
task.7.summaryItems.1.title: Single responsibility -
task.7.summaryItems.1.text: a method that performs exactly one task is easy to name and to trust.
task.7.summaryItems.2.title: Separation of concerns -
task.7.summaryItems.2.text: when a method performs two tasks, give one of them its own class or method.
task.7.summaryItems.3.title: Dependency injection -
task.7.summaryItems.3.text: let a class receive its collaborator through the constructor, so it can be substituted later.
task.7.summaryItems.4.title: Composition -
task.7.summaryItems.4.text: construct the parts, supply them, and let them collaborate - the shape of most production code.
task.7.summaryClose: Next you will meet these ideas by name in the design track: the single responsibility principle, and depending on what is supplied.
